articles.title: Indianapolis man who drove an old car, refused to own a cellphone and lived modestly for decades secretly amassed $13 million and left it to 12 local charities after his death
articles.summary: An Indianapolis man who spent decades living modestly, driving an old Honda and avoiding what he considered unnecessary expenses quietly accumulated a
articles.body: An Indianapolis man who spent decades living modestly, driving an old Honda and avoiding what he considered unnecessary expenses quietly accumulated a fortune worth more than $13 million. Terry Kahn, a retired US Department of Veterans Affairs employee, surprised his community after his death in January 2021, when his estate began distributing millions of dollars to approximately a dozen local charitable organisations. Despite his substantial wealth, Kahn had lived in the same modest house for more than two decades and even considered spending money on his own obituary unnecessary. His extraordinary legacy eventually benefited organisations supporting veterans, teachers, students, healthcare initiatives and children, with several nonprofits receiving donations worth approximately $1 million or more.Who was Terry Kahn, the Indianapolis man behind the $13 million fortune?Kahn was born in 1943 in Cleveland, Ohio, and grew up in Tucson, Arizona. He graduated from the University of Southern California with degrees in psychology and public administration before serving in the US Army during the Vietnam War and subsequently as an officer in the reserves.He moved to Indianapolis in 1976 and began working at the Richard L. Roudebush VA Medical Center. Over the following decades, he built a career with the Department of Veterans Affairs, eventually becoming its chief of human resources. He retired around 2003 after approximately 30 years of service.Beyond his professional life, Kahn was involved in community activities and supported several local organisations. He served on the board of the Health Foundation of Greater Indianapolis for more than 20 years and volunteered with Indiana Sports Corp.Despite his involvement in the community, Kahn rarely displayed the financial success he had achieved through years of saving and investing.Old Honda, no cellphone: How Kahn lived despite his multimillion-dollar wealthfering another indication of how modestly he had lived despite his substantial financial resources.However, his careful spending did not mean he avoided everything he enjoyed. Kahn was passionate about sports and maintained season tickets for the Indianapolis Colts, Indiana Pacers and Butler University men's basketball games. When he could not attend matches, he sold his tickets to recover the costs.How the frugal retiree secretly accumulated a $13 million fortuneKahn's wealth was built through decades of disciplined saving and investment, alongside an inheritance from his mother, who died around 2000.His attorney, Dwayne Isaacs, reportedly recalled that Kahn had accumulated approximately $3 million to $4 million when they first discussed his estate planning. By the time he died, the value of his estate had grown to more than $13 million.The fortune was particularly surprising to those who knew him because his spending habits gave little indication of his financial position.Kahn died on January 31, 2021, aged 77. His death revealed the extent of his wealth and the charitable intentions he had made arrangements for through his estate planning.Lawyer receives an unusual task of distributing millions to local charitiesAfter Kahn's death, his attorney Dwayne Isaacs and his former colleague and friend Vance McLarren took responsibility for distributing the estate's money.Rather than making numerous small contributions, the two decided to identify organisations where substantial donations could make a meaningful difference. They contacted nonprofits, examined their financial records, reviewed their work and assessed their ability to use the money effectively.The approach involved asking organisations what they would do with approximately $1 million.The unexpected offers initially left several charity representatives surprised. Some reportedly suspected that the calls and emails were scams and investigated the identities of the people contacting them before responding.Isaacs later revealed that three or four organisations missed out on the opportunity because they did not return his calls or take the offers seriously.Over approximately two years, the estate distributed more than $13 million among around a dozen Indianapolis-area charitable organisations.Teachers, veterans and children among beneficiaries of the $13 million estateThe donations supported organisations working across education, healthcare, housing, veterans' services and youth development. Several beneficiaries received contributions of approximately $1 million or more.Teachers' Treasures, an Indianapolis nonprofit that provides free school supplies to educators, received a reported $1.6 million from the estate. The contribution helped the organisation establish its first endowment fund, creating a longer-term financial resource for its work supporting teachers and students.Helping Veterans and Families of Indiana (HVAF), which provides housing and support services to veterans, received approximately $1 million. The organisation used part of the unrestricted contribution to address essential infrastructure requirements, including replacing an outdated heating and cooling system at a cost of approximately $250,000.Coburn Place, which supports survivors of domestic violence through housing and other services, also received more than $1 million. The contribution provided additional resources for its work with vulnerable individuals and families.The Arthur R. Baxter YMCA received $1.2 million. The organisation used the money to develop a soccer field and two smaller artificial-turf soccer parks, expanding recreational opportunities for children and young people in the community.Another beneficiary was the Washington Township Schools Foundation, which received $500,000 in August 2022. The contribution expanded its grants endowment, which was subsequently renamed the Ginny Hacker and Terry Kahn Grants Endowment. The fund was expected to make an additional $25,000 available annually for grants supporting teachers.Kahn's charitable legacy extended beyond his lifetimeKahn had maintained connections with several Indianapolis community organisations long before his death. His involvement with the Health Foundation of Greater Indianapolis and Indiana Sports Corp reflected his interest in local initiatives, education and community development.The estate's representatives sought to ensure that the donations supported organisations with established programmes and genuine financial needs. Rather than requiring beneficiaries to attach his name to buildings or projects, they allowed the organisations to use the money according to their priorities.His contributions consequently helped fund school supplies, teacher grants, veteran support services and sporting facilities, among other community initiatives.You use AI every day. articles.title: Australian man finds a strange 17-kg rock while searching for gold; years later, scientists identify it as a 4.6-billion-year-old meteorite; now held in a Victorian museum
articles.summary: A 17-kilogram reddish rock dug up in the state of Victoria turned out to be a space visitor, not the gold nugget its owner hoped for.
articles.body: A 17-kilogram reddish rock dug up in the state of Victoria turned out to be a space visitor, not the gold nugget its owner hoped for. Named the Maryborough meteorite after the nearby regional town, it formed about 4.6 billion years ago, around the birth of the solar system, which makes it slightly older than Earth. Its owner, David Hole, kept it for years believing a fortune lay inside, and it took a museum visit to settle the matter for good. It gave researchers a sample of material among the oldest available for study.How a gold prospector’s metal detector unearthed the Maryborough meteorite in a Victoria parkAccording to Futura-Sciences, Hole was prospecting with a metal detector in Maryborough Regional Park, about 1.9 kilometres south of the town, in May 2015. The area saw a gold rush in the 19th century and remains popular with amateur prospectors.Hole dug up an unusually heavy rock that he believed contained gold, but it resisted every attempt to open it. A saw, an angle grinder, a drill, acid and even blows from a sledgehammer all failed.Why Melbourne Museum geologists suspected the rock was a meteorite almost as soon as they saw itIntrigued, Hole took the rock to Melbourne Museum in 2018. Geologists Dermot Henry and Bill Birch suspected almost immediately that it was a meteorite. Its density was far greater than that of an Earth rock of the same size, and small depressions covered its surface.Henry told The Sydney Morning Herald in 2019 that the rock had a “sculpted, dimpled look”, while Birch told the newspaper that a rock like it on Earth should not be so heavy.Such a quick verdict was unusual. Futura-Sciences reported that Henry had examined many rocks brought in by owners convinced they were meteorites, and only two had ever turned out to be genuine. The museum cut a thin slice with a diamond saw for analysis, and Birch, Henry and geologist Andrew Tomkins published their findings, ‘Maryborough, a new H5 meteorite find from Victoria, Australia’, in July 2019 in the Proceedings of the Royal Society of Victoria.What scientists found inside the H5 ordinary chondrite that probably came from the asteroid beltThe meteorite is about 39 centimetres long and 14 centimetres wide and thick. It belongs to the ordinary chondrite family, the most common type of meteorite, which generally originates in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. Chondrites take their name from chondrules, small spherical silicate grains, here up to a millimetre across, that formed when dust in the young solar system briefly melted in a sudden heating event before solidifying.The letter H signals a high iron content, while the number 5 shows the rock was substantially heated inside its parent asteroid, so its matrix recrystallised and the chondrules became less distinct. The main metallic minerals are the iron-nickel alloys kamacite, taenite and tetrataenite, often found alongside an iron sulfide called troilite. The analysis showed no sign of a violent shock in space, and only thin layers of iron oxide around the metal grains, which suggests a relatively short time on Earth’s surface.When the Maryborough meteorite fell to Earth and why scientists value it more than any gold nuggetNobody knows exactly when the Maryborough meteorite landed, but carbon-14 dating at the University of Arizona points to a fall within the last 1,000 years, according to the Proceedings of the Royal Society of Victoria. The paper says the meteorite’s unweathered look suggests the lower end of that range, so people may have seen it fall. Newspapers reported bright meteors over the district between the late 19th and mid-20th centuries, including a 1923 letter to The Argus from a man whose surroundings were lit up so brightly that he was nearly dazzled. None of those reports can be linked to the find site, and there was no sign of an impact or of further fragments nearby when the paper was written.Gold prospectors have worked the area on and off since the late 19th century, yet if the meteorite lay on the surface then, it never drew enough curiosity for miners to take it to scientists. Nor is there evidence that Indigenous people interacted with it before European settlement.The paper calls Maryborough only the 17th meteorite recorded in Victoria and the ninth chondrite. Alongside the Dimboola and Pigick finds, it is the state’s third H5 ordinary chondrite, and the second-largest single chondrite mass after the 55-kilogram Kulnine. Museums Victoria later bought it from Hole, and it now sits in the museum’s collection. The authors add that it is perhaps surprising that more meteorites have not turned up in central Victoria since metal detecting for gold boomed in the 1970s, and the museum encourages prospectors to bring in unusual rocks for identification.You use AI every day. articles.title: SBI ordered to pay Rs 60,000 after delayed cheque clearance in Chhattisgarh; consumer panel rejects bank's unproven server-down defence, awards compensation and costs with interest
articles.summary: RAIPUR: The District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Rajnandgaon, has held the State Bank of India's local branch guilty of deficiency in service
articles.body: RAIPUR: The District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Rajnandgaon, has held the State Bank of India's local branch guilty of deficiency in service for failing to send a customer's cheque for clearing on time, leading to its dishonour as "out-dated".The bank has been directed to pay the cheque amount of Rs 50,000 along with compensation and costs. The Commission observed that the bank failed to prove the outage. The Commission noted that the bank had mentioned the server failure in its written reply but produced no documentary proof.With banking hours running from 10 am to 5 pm, the burden was on SBI to show that the server was down throughout working hours, and it did not discharge it.In an order on Thursday, the bench of President Prashant Kundu and Member Anand Varghese partly allowed the complaint filed by Khileshwar Sinha (48), a resident of Shanti Nagar, Ward 4, Rajnandgaon district, against the branch manager of SBI's Digvijay Stadium Campus branch on May 14, 2026.Sinha, an SBI account holder, received a Rs 50,000 cheque from Ravi Vaishnav, drawn on Jana Small Finance Bank Ltd's Durg branch and dated Nov 21, 2025. He deposited it at his SBI branch on Feb 18, 2026, within the validity period, and said he had also alerted a bank employee.According to the complaint, the bank did not send the cheque for clearing on Feb 19, a working day, and sent it only on Feb 20, two days later. It was returned on Feb 21 with a memo stamped "instrument out-dated" (stale). Sinha called this "complete negligence" and sought the cheque amount, Rs 10,000 for mental agony and litigation costs, and other relief under Section 35 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.SBI argued that a technical fault, network problem and system outage on Feb 19 prevented the cheque from being sent for clearing. It said the cheque was sent on Feb 20 and returned as stale because 90 days had passed since its issuance, and that the bank was not negligent.It also claimed it had asked Sinha to get a fresh date put on the cheque and redeposit it, but he instead approached the Commission. It sought dismissal of the complaint. The bank's only evidence was the affidavit of its representative, Jadbendra Kapa.The complainant deposited the cheque on the 88th day after its issuance, well within the permitted period, the Commission noted.By not sending the cheque for clearing on time, the bank allowed it to lapse. The bench held that failure to present a cheque on time, leading to its expiry, was clear negligence and a deficiency in service.The order relied on the Supreme Court's ruling in Canara Bank vs Kavita Chaudhary (2026 INSC 363, dated April 15, 2026), as cited in the order.It held that a bank's failure to present or collect a cheque in time, resulting in its expiry, amounts to serious negligence and deficiency in service. The Court also said banks cannot shelter behind internal technical reasons or routine excuses, and are answerable if a customer suffers legal or financial loss.Holding that the customer was entitled to the cheque amount, the Commission recognised that non-realisation of the money would naturally cause mental distress. It awarded Rs 10,000 against the Rs 10,000 claimed for mental agony and costs, split equally.The bank must pay Rs 50,000, the cheque amount, Rs 5,000 as compensation for mental agony, and Rs 5,000 as litigation costs. The Commission also directed the bank to pay interest at 6% per annum from Nov 26, 2026, until payment.If payment is not made within 45 days, the bank will have to pay interest at 9% per annum from the date of the order until payment.The ruling underlines that banks handling cheques for collection carry a duty of timely action, and that a "technical glitch" defence needs documentary backing to stand before a consumer forum.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Raipur | Silver Rate in Raipur | Bank Holidays in Raipur | Public Holidays in Raipur | Raipur AQI | Weather in Raipur | Petrol Price in Raipur | Diesel Price in Raipur | CNG Price in Raipur | LPG Price in RaipurStay updated with the latest Raipur news. articles.title: The Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade is on for Saturday. One high school band had to scramble an extra $350,000 to make it.
articles.summary: Here's what we know about who is scheduled to perform at the delayed parade after a nor'easter forced its first-ever postponement.
articles.body:
The Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade will go ahead Saturday after being postponed earlier this week for the first time in its history.

The lineup was announced this month, but the participation of some performers was thrown into doubt when a fierce nor'easter forced the parade to be delayed .

The parade's executive producer, Will Coss, said on Thursday that there had been an "overwhelmingly positive response" from the performers as organizers tried to resolve issues.

"We're actively working through all the pieces of our parade, but I have to say there's an overwhelming positive response," he told TODAY. "Our performers, our talent, our performance groups, our bands… we're all coming together to try to figure this out. We're optimistic we're going to have a really successful parade on Saturday morning."

According to the list of performers on broadcast partner NBC's website , Grammy-nominated acts RAYE, Teddy Swims and country singer Megan Moroney are set to perform. Other headliners include Queen Latifah, Keke Palmer, Jimmy Fallon & The Roots and JoJo.

The wider line-up includes EJAE, Indigo Girls, Natalie Merchant, Baha Men, Natasha Bedingfield, Blues Traveler, DEVO, Feid, Icona Pop, Il Volo, Wyclef Jean, Jamie Miller, RIIZE and Smash Mouth.

There is also a tribute to the late Queen of country, Dolly Parton, led by Megan Hilty.

Broadway stars Leslie Odom Jr. and Anthony Ramos are also performing, as is Hunger Games actor Mckenna Grace. Special appearances are said to be planned from Jack McBrayer, Janet McTeer, John Stamos, Melissa Joan Hart, as well as Holly Robinson Peete and Rodney Peete.

The all-star Broadway medley is going ahead, according to Deadline , with performers from The Lost Boys, The Rocky Horror Show, Wicked, Schmigadoon!, Aladdin, The Book of Mormon and Chicago confirmed. Paddington the Musical will appear on a separate float.

Macy's has not yet confirmed that every act can make the new date.

Several bands have scrambled to stay in New York for the rescheduled parade, with some raising money for their extended stay in a matter of hours.

The Pride of Pearland band from Texas raised an extra $350,000 in under 24 hours to extend its stay.

"Because of YOU, the Pride of Pearland Band & Color Guard has met our fundraising goal to cover the unexpected costs of extra days in New York City," it posted on Instagram. "To everyone who donated, shared our story, made a call or sent encouragement—THANK YOU. You helped make it possible for our 500+ students to stay and experience the moment they've worked so hard for.

Elsewhere, the Concord Community High School Marching Minutemen from Elkhart, Ind., were already planning to be in the New York area through Saturday, so their plans are unaffected.

Dobyns-Bennett High School from Kingsport, Tenn., is reported to have secured the extra funding it needed, as has James F. Byrnes High School from Duncan, S.C., which met its funding goal. The University of Illinois Marching Illini are also staying, after launching a fundraiser to cover an extra $175,000 in costs.

The Nā Koa Aliʻi Hawaiʻi All-State band is staying too, with the band telling Hawaii News Now it has raised $500,000 of the $700,000 it needs to cover its costs so far.

The University of Connecticut band is also staying, and said it will make its first-ever appearance at the parade thanks to generous donors.

Not everyone can stay, though, with the University of Alabama's Million Dollar Band returning to Tuscaloosa for the Iron Bowl, which kicks off at 6:30 p.m. Saturday.

Macy's Great American Marching Band is also unable to take part, according to NBC , after they couldn't make the new date work financially.

Individual performers have been affected as well. Cheerleader Lola Smith of Phoenix is staying to perform with Spirit of America cheer, but other members of the Mesa, Ariz. group are not, AZ Family reported.

The parade steps off at 8:30 a.m. ET Saturday and is broadcast on NBC, Peacock and Telemundo.

The 2.5-mile route runs from the Upper West Side down to Macy's Herald Square flagship store at 34th Street and Seventh Avenue.

It usually wraps up by noon. NBC will also air an encore presentation at 2 p.m.

articles.title: Bangladesh labour unrest: Zara, H&M among brands shifting orders to India, other Asian hubs
articles.summary: The ongoing labour unrest in Bangladesh prompted global fashion retailers, including Zara and H&M, to shift a significant share of their orders to other
articles.body: The ongoing labour unrest in Bangladesh prompted global fashion retailers, including Zara and H&M, to shift a significant share of their orders to other Asian manufacturing hubs in the first half of November, Reuters reported, citing factory owners.The orders, diverted between November 1-18, accounted for about one-tenth of their total orders and were valued at around $254 million.Most of the diverted orders went to India, while buyers also turned to Vietnam, Cambodia and Indonesia to minimise supply-chain risks and ensure more reliable deliveries.Industry leaders in Bangladesh say rising wages, energy shortages and political uncertainty have eroded the country's low-cost advantage, which helped establish it as the world's second-largest apparel exporter after China.According to the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association, the protests have resulted in production losses exceeding $400 million. The garment industry accounts for more than 80% of the country's export earnings and nearly 40% of its manufacturing jobs.Minimum wage hike fails to ease unrestThe pressure on Bangladesh's garment industry intensified on Wednesday after the government approved a 36% increase in the minimum wage for garment workers, the smallest hike in four decades.The increase fell significantly short of workers' demand for more than double their existing wages, triggering fresh clashes with police. However, Abdur Rahman Tarafder, secretary of the ministry of labour and employment, described the hike as "satisfactory" and expressed hope that all workers would resume work from Saturday.Industry leaders said the wage increase would nevertheless narrow Bangladesh's labour-cost advantage over India. Trade unions, however, maintained that the revised wages remained low by global industry standards.Factory owners, who spoke on condition of anonymity over concerns about their relationships with international buyers, said the unrest had prompted global brands, including Zara, H&M, Marks & Spencer and Celio, to divert orders to other countries, with India receiving the bulk of the business.Energy shortages and delivery delays disrupt garment productionFactory owners said their bigger concern was that the shift in business to other countries could become permanent, even after the situation in Bangladesh stabilises.Persistent energy shortages, worsened by the Middle East crisis, have further disrupted production and forced some factories to depend on more expensive alternative power sources.India can offer buyers a delivery advantage of about a week, while Vietnam and Cambodia can reduce lead times by as much as 15 days.Rival sourcing hubs can typically complete production and delivery within 60 to 90 days, compared with around 120 days in Bangladesh.The disruptions have also led to production backlogs, with manufacturers around Dhaka losing an estimated 20 to 25 production days. Some factories are considering overtime and air freight to meet delivery commitments.Political tensions surrounding former prime minister Sheikh Hasina's possible return to Dhaka from India have also added to concerns over further disruption.Industry leaders have called for stability and uninterrupted production to retain international buyers.You use AI every day. articles.title: Charity shop reunites Mel Giedroyc with jacket from her uni days
articles.summary: The comedian and presenter's name was sewn into the jacket and spotted by a charity shop manager.
articles.body:
Nearly 40 years after it disappeared, comedian and presenter Mel Giedroyc has been reunited with a leather jacket she wore "every single day at university" after it appeared at a charity shop.

Zoey Kennedy, manager at Oxfam in Stroud, said she was straightening out the tartan lining of the jacket when she became "very excited".

"On the name tag was Melanie Giedroyc and I thought, could that be?" Kennedy said.

After making a trip to Gloucestershire to be reunited with the jacket, the former Great British Bake Off star said: "I wore this jacket every single day at university; I thought I was a little bit cool, a little bit rock and roll. Then it disappeared out of my life; I can't remember how."

'If we get E. coli from 52-year-old pudding, so be it'

Murdered woman's father welcomes new stalking law

Female gamers told to 'get back in kitchen'

The original 1950s Highwayman leather jacket, bought at a London market, features a painted dog and the name of the rock band The Dogs D'Amour on the back, as Mel's sister was involved in one of the band's music videos.

"I thought [two] things, one was that it would be really exciting if it was [Giedroyc's], but also we laughed a bit that it's so not cool to have your name sewn in a leather jacket that was, obviously, a very cool item," Kennedy said.

Oxfam got in touch with Giedroyc, 58, through her agent, who confirmed it was her jacket.

Kennedy said Giedroyc tried it on in the shop and said it was heavier than she remembered and the colour had "held up really well".

"It still smells the same," the presenter said.

"The name tag's still there, zips everywhere; it still fits!"

Despite the happy reunion, the jacket's journey to Oxfam remains a mystery, and Giedroyc has not taken it home.

Instead, Kennedy said she wants it to find a new home through the charity shop.

"It should go to somebody who is cool enough to wear The Dogs D'Amour on the back," Giedroyc said.

Kennedy said Giedroyc was "so lovely, really friendly, just happy to be there".

"She's a big supporter of pre-loved clothes and has always said how much she supports recycling and all the things Oxfam do so well," she said.

"We were just really pleased that she came down, had a look round and she was just a joy to have in the shop."

articles.title: Tory candidates must commit to  scrapping net-zero targets, says Kemi Badenoch
articles.summary: The Tory leader says her "candidates covenant" would build trust in the party, but some ex-MPs have criticised the move.
articles.body:
All Conservative candidates will have to sign a pledge committing themselves to leaving the European Convention on Human Rights and scrapping net-zero emission targets ahead of the next election, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has said.

Unveiling her "candidates covenant" at an event in the East Midlands, Badenoch said both policies were "necessary for a stronger economy and a stronger country".

The move could see some senior Conservatives blocked from standing for the party at the next general election.

Lord Barwell, a former Conservative minister and No 10 chief of staff, said: "After a summer in which the impacts of climate change were clearer than ever, this is bad policy."

He added: "Given the seats Conservative strategists say they are targeting, it is also bad politics."

Tobias Ellwood, a former Conservative MP and defence minister, told Matt Chorley on BBC Radio 5Live he had applied to stand as a candidate in the next election but had not passed what he described as "the purity test".

He criticised Badenoch's covenant, saying: "Can you imagine if... prior to the war, you had to sign up to [Neville] Chamberlain's 'peace in our time' speech, you know, [Winston] Churchill wouldn't have been allowed to stand."

"I mean, there must be times where you can have different views and different views within a party are actually helpful," he added.

Addressing party activists in Newark, Badenoch said: "The government that cleans up Andy Burnham's mess is going to have to make some very difficult decisions... it is not going to be for the faint-hearted.

"I need everyone who stands as a Conservative candidate at the next election to know what they are standing for - I don't want to hear complaining from MPs that they didn't know what we were going to do."

The covenant also states that candidates must support staying out of the EU, reducing the size of the state and changing the welfare system.

Sir Mark Spencer, a chief whip in the last Conservative government, became the first to sign the new pledge.

He lost his seat in the 2024 election, but is now standing in Newark, where he hopes to unseat the Conservative-turned-Reform UK MP Robert Jenrick.

A Labour spokesperson said: "Kemi Badenoch is living in an alternate reality. She says the Tories have changed but the truth is they're the same old Tories."

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said: "Kemi Badenoch tells us the Conservative Party has changed - it's hard to believe when she's surrounded by so many Remainers and her party is selecting lots of failed ex-Tory MPs who got kicked out at the last election."

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said: "The Conservatives pretend they care about winning back support from millions of former Conservative voters, yet Kemi Badenoch is now asking her candidates to sign the 'Farage pact'.

Net zero by 2050 'impossible' for UK, says Badenoch

UK will leave ECHR if Tories win election, Badenoch says

Shapps blocked from standing again for the Conservatives

Both the commitments to leave the ECHR and repeal net-zero targets represent a shift from previous Conservative governments.

The net-zero target was originally legislated for by the Theresa May-led Conservative government in 2019. The party's 2024 manifesto said it was proud of its record on reducing emissions and remained "committed to delivering net-zero by 2050".

In the run-up to the election, then Prime Minister, and Conservative leader, Rishi Sunak resisted demands from some in his party to commit to leaving the ECHR.

Since becoming leader, Badenoch has argued that the net-zero target - which commits the UK to reducing its net greenhouse gas emissions to almost zero by 2050 - couldn't be achieved "without a serious drop in our living standards or by bankrupting us".

Last year, she also announced that, if elected, her party would take the UK out of the European Convention on Human Rights, the treaty that guarantees certain human rights such as the right to privacy, protection against torture and a right to a family life.

Badenoch said the convention prevented the UK from being able to secure its borders and deport foreign criminals.

Over the past year, the Labour government, along with other European countries have agreed to negotiate a new approach to the convention with the aim of making it easier to deport people.

articles.title: A 3,400-year-old Egyptian dump yielded 40 pierced papyrus fragments; their burn marks reveal a curse ritual against the serpent Apophis
articles.summary: Discover the significance of 3,400-year-old papyrus fragments found in Egypt, revealing ancient rituals against the chaotic serpent Apophis and the sun god Re.
articles.body: A collection of about 40 papyrus fragments was found in an ancient rubbish dump in Egypt. With the help of this recovery, archaeologists got rare physical evidence of a rite, which was intended to destroy one of Egyptian mythology’s most feared figures. These fragments could be dated back more than 3,400 years and had drawings and inscriptions which were linked with Apophis, the serpent of chaos. The Egyptian sun god, Re, was believed to be threatened by Apophis during his nightly journey through the underworld. With several pieces bearing the signs of piercing and burning, researchers believed that these were used in ceremonies which were designed to symbolically defeat the serpent of chaos.During an excavation at the mortuary temple of Pharaoh Thutmose III, these papyrus fragments were discovered. When the drawings and inscriptions were compared with descriptions of the ritual by the researchers, the significance of the findings became clearer. The physical damage matched the descriptions of the ritual that were preserved in a much later written Egyptian text. This implied that the practice was already there during the New Kingdom, meaning years before the surviving detailed instructions were noted down.What the collection found implies about the ritualIn Egyptian mythology, Apophis, who is also known as Apep, was seen as the representative of chaos and disorder. People at the time believed that the giant serpent attacked the sun god Re during his travels through the underworld at night. People believed that this threatened the continuation of the daily cycle of sunrise. Hence, rituals that were intended to repel or overthrow Apophis had a purpose; that is, they symbolically helped protect the sun god and preserve the original order of the world.The ceremony was reportedly known as Overthrowing Apophis. In the surviving materials, researchers observed two major groups: one containing depictions of Apophis himself and the other one containing figures who have been referred to as the “Children of the Rebel.” As per the University of Copenhagen’s research, out of the 40 fragments uncovered, 12 were identified as belonging to the Apophis group, and 14 belonged to the second category. The remaining fragments hadn’t been classified yet, as they were incomplete.Notably, the surviving fragments were written in ink, which was generally the colour used in Egyptian religious contexts to refer to dangerous or hostile forces. Some pieces even include red dividing lines, leading researchers to guess that possibly larger sheets of papyrus were divided into smaller sections before being cut up.Aside from this, some of the pieces indicate punctures that are similar to stabbing marks. Such traces were considered important because the later ritual text describes the destruction of representations of Apophis via actions which include piercing and burning,Why does the rubbish dump hold such importance?Fragments were recovered over several years. The earliest of them was found in 2014, while the latest was in 2025. As the pieces were found, a deposit outside the enclosure wall of Thutmose III’s mortuary temple, researchers believe that the ritual materials were likely present inside the temple before being discarded outside.Moreover, these Egyptian execration practices could have been used to counter other perceived personal threats. The University of Copenhagen’s research suggested that such rituals could also be associated with attempts to secure personal success or even cause harm to an enemy. Therefore, the papyri provide a direct connection between Egyptian texts and the physical actions that were likely carried out during the practices. Instead of simply relying on the written descriptions, researchers can now examine objects that appear to have been prepared, damaged and discarded as part of the ritual itself, thus offering a rare glimpse of how the Egyptians translated their belief in the struggle against chaos into repeated, material acts more than three millennia ago.You use AI every day. articles.title: Police look for more than 100 gig-goers to help Co-op Live investigation
articles.summary: Rap fans say people were "choking" and "coughing up blood" towards the end of Don Toliver's gig.
articles.body:
Police have said they are trying to contact more than 100 gig-goers to help their investigation after an unknown substance was released at a concert at Manchester's Co-op Live arena.

Detectives believe a "small group of organised criminals targeted people in the crowd to commit a series of robberies on the night".

More than 12,000 people were evacuated from the arena during a performance by US rapper Don Toliver on Sunday.

One woman was taken to hospital and 88 others were treated at the scene after concertgoers reported a "horrible smell" and some people "coughing up blood".

No arrests have been made and the substance has not yet been identified.

Assistant Chief Constable Tom Harding said: "We're working to identify those [robbery] suspects and the substance that we believe was released in the crowd as part of these incidents.

He said there had been "similar incidents at two Don Toliver gigs in Europe that are also relevant to our enquiries".

Fans reported that a spray or gas was released into the crowd in Zurich and Paris.

GMP previously said there had been nine reports of jewellery being stolen during the concert.

Harding said officers had been "working through footage captured on mobile phones and CCTV".

He added: "There are over a hundred people at the gig that we are working to try and contact to potentially assist with our enquiries.

"We thank all those that have assisted us so far.

"We also know many more people were impacted on the night and afterwards, physically and psychologically."

North West Ambulance Service said it had deployed crews, including its Hazardous Area Response Team, who carried out decontamination "as a precaution".

Those who suffered symptoms had been taken to the Etihad stadium.

Some fans complained the process, which involved them changing into paper white suits and putting their clothes in a plastic bag, was "invasive" and "traumatic".

Many stayed quarantined for several hours before being able to leave in the early hours of Monday.

GMP said: "People's safety, and the safety of the wider community, was at the forefront of officers' minds throughout."

The substance was released at about 22:00 GMT, near the end of Toliver's show as part of his Nitrous – Octane world tour.

Concertgoers have described feeling "unsafe" and seeing "distressing" scenes and people "coughing up blood".

Posting on Instagram, Toliver said: "My heart and prayers are with everyone that was injured.

"The only thing I love more than creating music is performing for my fans."

Co-op Live, which reopened its doors on Thursday night for a gig by American singer Phoebe Bridgers, previously said its priority remained "the safety and security of all visitors" to the venue.

articles.title: In 1912, stranded in Antarctica, Captain Scott wrote that his team would “die like gentlemen”; his farewell letter later sold for £163,250
articles.summary: Discover the poignant farewell letter of Captain Robert Falcon Scott, written in 1912 during his ill-fated Antarctic expedition, which sold for an astonishing £163,250 at auction. Explore the tragic story behind this historical document.
articles.body: In March 1912, British explorer Captain Robert Falcon Scott was attempting to make the journey back from the South Pole with the surviving members of his crew. One of his companions had already lost his life, while another had walked away into a blizzard. The remaining men with him were struggling against exhaustion, hunger and extreme cold. On March 16, the Captain wrote to his friend and expedition supporter, Sir Edgar Speyer, acknowledging that the party might not survive. He wrote, as cited by Sky News, “I fear we must go and that it leaves the Expedition in a bad muddle.But we have been to the Pole, and we shall die like gentlemen.” The four-page handwritten letter was eventually recovered with Scott’s body and later sold at an auction in 2012.The race to the South Pole and the difficult journey backThis expedition by Scott is officially known as the British Antarctic Expedition of 1910-1913. More commonly, it is also known as the Terra Nova, after its ship. Alongside the ambition of reaching the South Pole, this expedition also had some scientific objectives. The journey turned into a race when Norwegian explorer Roald Amundsen also set out for the southernmost point of the Earth. On December 14, 1911, Amundsen’s party reached the Pole. Scott and his party arrived on January 17, 1912 and found evidence that the Norwegian party had been there prior to them.Scott’s party began their way back on January 19. Their route back across the Antarctic landscape was difficult, and their conditions only deteriorated with time. According to the University of Cambridge’s database, Petty Officer Edgar Evans lost his life on February 17, near the foot of the Beardmore Glacier. Captain Lawrence Oates, on the other hand, was suffering severely by March from frostbite and could no longer keep pace with the rest of them. On March 16, during a blizzard, he left the tent after informing his companions that he was just going outside and might take him some time to be back. He never returned.The remaining team, including Scott, Dr Edward Wilson and Lieutenant Henry Bowers, continued their journey north, making their final camp around March 19. They were around 11 miles away from One Ton Depot, a point that contained food and fuel. However, a prolonged blizzard prevented them from reaching it. With the remaining provisions dwindling, the three men became too weak to continue forward. Scott’s letter to Speyer was dated three days before their final camp was established; therefore, it can be assumed that it belonged to the period when the party was still attempting to make its way back.What the letter containedDated March 16, 1912, the letter was addressed to financier and supporter Edgar Speyer, who had helped fund the expedition. In the letter, Scott expressed understanding that they might never make it back and mentioned regret for the women they would leave behind. He also expressed his gratitude towards Speyer for his assistance. In addition to this, Scott hoped that if his diary was ever found, it would show how the men had remained with their sick companions and continued fighting till the very end.The Captain’s diary was later found alongside their bodies by a search party that was led by Surgeon Edward Atkinson on November 12, 1912. The final entry was dated March 29. He, Wilson and Bowers died in their tent during the final days of March, from starvation and cold. The party collected the records and personal belongings, and the letters were then sent to their intended recipients.The letter sold for £163,250 at an auctionBefore being offered at Bonhams’ Polar Sale in London in 2012, the letter to Speyer had remained in private hands. The four-page letter was catalogued as a farewell letter written shortly after Oates disappeared into the blizzard and only days before Scott’s party established the final camp. Its estimated value was £100,000 to £150,000. It, however, sold for £163,250, thus exceeding the estimated value. Sky News reported that an anonymous British collector bought the letter at the auction.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 'Brought disgrace to Tamil Nadu': Stalin targets TVK govt after Supreme Court's Deepam rebuke
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: DMK chief MK Stalin on Friday accused the TVK-led Tamil Nadu government of bringing \"disgrace\" to the state by failing to present a strong
articles.body: NEW DELHI: DMK chief MK Stalin on Friday accused the TVK-led Tamil Nadu government of bringing "disgrace" to the state by failing to present a strong defence before the Supreme Court in the Deepam case.His remarks came hours after the Supreme Court came down heavily on the Tamil Nadu government for defying its order in the case, observing that it was prima facie in contempt of court."The incompetent TVK government has brought unprecedented peril to Tamil Nadu’s history—threatening our traditions, religious harmony, and state rights! The Supreme Court verdict in the Thiruparankundram matter is a blatant defeat for the TVK government!" Stalin wrote in Tamil on X."The Supreme Court has ordered that a lamp be lit tomorrow on a pillar atop the Tirupparankundram hill. The incompetent Vijay administration has brought disgrace to Tamil Nadu by failing to present strong arguments in court," the former chief minister added.Stalin termed the Supreme Court's directives, including handing over security of the Thiruparankundram temple and hill to the CRPF, suspending its board of trustees, appointing two former judges to oversee its management and summoning senior officials, a "shock."He also likened the TVK government's handling of the issue to a monkey mishandling a delicate flower garland and accused it of using the temple's board of trustees as a shield."The Dravidian movement—through sixty years of struggle, bloodshed, and the sacrifice of many lives—had secured and safeguarded state rights, which were once in the hands of fraudulent groups—under the control of democratic governance. Now, through a single legal case, all of this has been surrendered to the Union government," Stalin said.The DMK supremo cited chief minister C Joseph Vijay's lack of political experience, given his background as a Tamil film superstar before entering politics, but maintained that the real problem was his "reluctance" to allow experienced and knowledgeable people to get close to him.Stalin described Vijay's silence on the issue as a "historic betrayal" of Tamil Nadu.The Supreme Court's order followed the authorities' failure to allow the ceremonial lighting of the Karthigai Deepam lamp atop the Deepathoon in Madurai, despite the court's one-time directive issued on November 20. articles.title: During WWII, an Australian couple exchanged nearly 500 love letters; hidden beneath their home for decades, they resurfaced after both parents had died and showed their daughter a romance she never knew
articles.summary: Lynne Smith discovers nearly 500 love letters exchanged between her parents during World War II, revealing a romantic side of her parents that she never knew of.
articles.body: During the Second World War, letters were one of the primary ways military personnel communicated with their families. Imagine stumbling across a hidden box of letters that narrate a love story; who wouldn’t want to read them? For Queenslander Lynne Smith, that scenario became a reality when she was reunited with her parents’ wartime letters after the new owners of her former family home stumbled across them.Smith was completely stunned when someone reached out to her regarding an accidental find at her former family home. According to Kids News, the major discovery was a box of love letters penned by her parents, Fred and Elwyn Mortley, during World War II. Smith gushed over the discovery, saying, “It’s amazing. I never knew they existed.”A major discovery in the basement As Smith explained, her parents were a private couple who never talked about their past. She knew that they got engaged during the Second World War, married afterward, and built a house on Sydney’s Northern Beaches. Beyond knowing that they treated each other with great respect, she knew very little about their early relationship.Growing up, Smith’s only glimpse into her parents’ romance was her mother’s short diary entries: “Received a letter from Fred.” Over the years, she often wondered what they had written to each other while her father was on duty, assuming she would never find out since her reserved parents had passed away nearly three decades earlier. When the family house was eventually sold, no sign of their letters was found.However, a turning point came in October 2024, when the current homeowners took to social media to appeal for help locating any surviving members of the Mortley family after stumbling across a box hidden in the home’s basement. It contained letters addressed to Sergeant F. Mortley and Elwyn B. Wombold. A friend of Smith’s noticed the post and contacted her right away.Overcome with emotion, Smith immediately calledher sons and a few close friends who had known her parents well. Even after 80 years, the letters were in good condition, bundled together with twine and thread, and covered in sprawling handwriting. Because Smith resided far away from her childhood home at the time and hadn’t yet had the opportunity to read all the letters, she granted the Sydney newspaper The Daily Telegraph first access to examine them. What the letters revealed was an epic romance.Inside the wartime lettersIn a love note dated January 1945, written while sitting in an army barracks, 27-year-old Fred wrote tothen-20-year-old Elwyn, “I do long for the day when I can actually hold you in my arms and kiss you till my heart sings.” Meanwhile, Elwyn, whom Smith remembered as a strict and serious mother, wrote her letter like a playful young woman, flirting with her fiancé and yearning for his safe return. “Hello sweetheart, are you behaving yourself tonight? I hope not taking any strange women out seeing it is our Wednesday night,” Elwyn penned.While they were always kind to each other, Smith recalled that they never displayed public affection or acted touchy in front of her. Across nearly 500 letters, the couple documented everyday life in the middle of World War II. In a letter dated August 24, 1945, Elwyn joked to Fred that the full moon had driven her mad. In another, Fred teased Elwyn for cheering for a rival regional football team. As for how the letters survived over eight decades, Smith believed her father intentionally tucked them away, hoping his children would eventually find them.You use AI every day. articles.body: An Australian worker earning A$155,000 a year has won an unfair dismissal case after his employer partly blamed artificial intelligence tools for making his position unnecessary. The Fair Work Commission found that the company no longer needed his job, but ruled that his dismissal was unfair because he could reasonably have been moved into another vacant position. Commissioner McKinnon ordered LVL80 SLR Pty Ltd to pay the former employee A$17,861.54 in compensation. Of this amount, A$12,115.39 must be paid directly to the worker, while A$5,746.15 must go into his superannuation account. The decision was known as Basic v LVL80 SLR Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4327 and was delivered in Sydney earlier this month on 6 November. It shows an important point for employers: even when a job is genuinely no longer needed, they must consider whether an affected employee could reasonably move into another available role before ending their employment.The road to redundancy: A meeting with AIThe worker was employed as a contracts administrator by LVL80 and its earlier businesses from 10 January 2022. He earned A$155,000 a year, plus superannuation. In June 2025, LVL80 Cranes Pty Ltd bought the business of Titan Group. On 16 June that year, Titan employees, including the worker, moved to the LVL80 Group. The worker put in long hours, including weekends, to help transfer contracts to the new company. The employer later said business activity had fallen and some of the worker's duties could be handled using artificial intelligence tools. It also said there was no longer a need for a contracts administrator. LVL80 made the worker's position redundant on 18 May 2026, and his employment ended on the same day.The worker argued that his work had not disappeared. He said some of his duties had been passed to other employees, including people in the company's legal function. He also argued that contract negotiations could not be fully handled by AI. The Commission accepted that some duties had been shared among other employees. However, Commissioner McKinnon said this did not prove the redundancy was not genuine. Sharing work among staff can be a normal part of changes to how a business operates. An internal email sent six days before the dismissal said the number of quotes had fallen by more than half and that the worker's workload was well below its level a year earlier. The Commissioner accepted that LVL80 no longer needed anyone to perform the contracts administrator role.The unfair dismissal claim: AI vs. realityThe worker challenged his dismissal through the Fair Work Commission, arguing that the company had not handled the process fairly. Under Australia's Fair Work Act 2009, a genuine redundancy must meet specific requirements. These include that the employer no longer needs the job to be done by anyone because of changes to its business operations. The employer must also meet any relevant consultation rules and consider whether it would have been reasonable to move the employee into another role within the business or an associated company. In this case, the Commission accepted that the contracts administrator position was no longer required. However, that was not the end of the matter. The law also required LVL80 to consider whether the worker could have been redeployed elsewhere in the business. The worker said the company had not properly considered this option and had not given him a real chance to discuss other available jobs. That issue became central to the Commission's decision.The vacant role that changed the outcomeDuring the redundancy meeting on 18 May 2026, LVL80 told the worker about three vacant positions. He showed interest in a sales role, but the company told him that none of the available jobs matched his skills and qualifications. One of the positions was a Sales and Operations Administrator role based in South Australia. It had been advertised as a full-time job, with a starting salary of between A$75,000 and A$85,000. LVL80 argued that the worker was not suitable for the vacancies and said the sales position was part-time. The company also accepted that, apart from telling him why it considered each role unsuitable, it had not discussed redeployment with him. The Commissioner found that moving the worker into the Sales and Operations Administrator position would have been reasonable. Although the job involved a lower salary and would have been a step down, the worker's existing skills could be adapted to the duties.The Commission also accepted his evidence that he would have considered moving interstate and taking a lower salary to remain employed. He had ongoing mortgage and child support payments, and the Commissioner found that accepting a less senior role would have been a better option than losing his job altogether. LVL80 later filled the position on a part-time basis. However, the Commissioner was not convinced that the company had intended the job to be part-time when the worker was dismissed. Because the employer had not properly considered this reasonable redeployment option, the dismissal did not meet the genuine redundancy test under section 389(2) of the Fair Work Act 2009.Tribunal decision: Redundancy process found unfairThe Commission found that LVL80 had a valid business reason for making the worker's position redundant. The company had made at least 13 employees redundant since June 2025, and the Commissioner rejected the worker's suggestion that a complaint he had made about a colleague in 2025 played a significant part in the decision. However, the way the company handled the dismissal was unreasonable.LVL80 held only one meeting with the worker about the redundancy. It lasted between 10 and 30 minutes, and the company had already decided to end his employment before the meeting began. The Commissioner found that the worker had received no prior warning and had not been properly involved in discussions about other jobs he might have taken. This meant he had no real chance to influence the decision or prepare for the loss of his employment.The company had 30 employees, while the wider LVL80 Group had about 150. The Commission also found that the business had access to human resources expertise, including through its senior legal counsel. The decision did not establish that the company had used AI as a false excuse to remove the worker. Instead, it found that the job itself was no longer needed, but that the employer had failed to properly consider a reasonable alternative before dismissing him.Compensation and industry impactThe worker did not ask to return to his former position, and the sales and operations administrator job had already been filled. The Commissioner estimated that the worker would have stayed in the sales position for about six months while looking for a better job. The calculation included four weeks of earnings at his former salary and another 22 weeks at the sales role's annual salary of A$85,000. This produced estimated earnings of about A$47,884.62, plus A$5,746.15 in superannuation. The Commission then deducted A$35,769.23 that the worker had already received when his employment ended. This covered four weeks of pay in place of notice and eight weeks of redundancy pay. The resulting compensation was A$17,861.54, with A$12,115.39 payable directly to the worker and A$5,746.15 paid into his superannuation account.The decision offers an important lesson for employers considering job cuts involving AI and other new technology. A company may be able to show that a role is no longer needed, even if some of its duties are taken over by software or shared among other workers. But it must still properly examine whether the employee can move into another vacant position. That role does not have to offer the same pay or seniority. In this case, the Commission found that an interstate job with a much lower salary was a reasonable option because the worker was willing to consider relocating and accepting less money.The ruling also shows why employers should not make a final decision before speaking properly with an affected employee. LVL80 had a valid reason for removing the contracts administrator position, but its failure to give the worker a genuine chance to discuss another job made the dismissal unfair. The case therefore does not mean that employers cannot use AI as part of a restructuring or make jobs redundant when technology changes the way work is done. It shows that they must still follow the law, consider available positions and give employees a fair opportunity to discuss alternatives before their employment ends.You use AI every day. articles.title: From $24.6 billion to $1.7 billion: Billionaire Carl Icahn loses 93% of his fortune in five years, with $1.4 billion in debt, failed market bets putting his business empire under financial pressure
articles.summary: Carl Icahn has lost roughly 93% of his fortune in five years, with his net worth falling from $24.6 billion to around $1.7 billion.
articles.body: Carl Icahn has lost roughly 93% of his fortune in five years, with his net worth falling from $24.6 billion to around $1.7 billion. The 90-year-old billionaire's decline comes at a time when the wider US stock market has surged, making the reversal particularly striking. Now, with $1.4 billion in bonds coming due next May and refinancing concerns mounting, the veteran corporate raider faces another test of his business empire.According to Forbes data, Icahn's fortune has fallen to its lowest level since 1997, nearly three decades ago. The Queens-born financier, once ranked the world's 26th-richest person in 2021, has seen roughly $23 billion wiped from his wealth over the past five years.Icahn's fortune falls as Wall Street ralliesThe scale of the decline stands out against the performance of the broader market. Since late November 2021, the Dow has climbed around 40% to 46%, the Nasdaq has gained approximately 50% to 53%, and the S&P 500 has risen between 53% and 58%, supported in part by the artificial intelligence boom.Icahn, meanwhile, was hurt by bearish market bets that went against him. His wealth is largely tied to units of Icahn Enterprises, the publicly traded company whose investments have suffered years of losses. The units fell another 56% this quarter, according to SEC filings.The impact has been compounded by personal borrowing. Icahn pledged his company units as collateral for $1.3 billion in personal loans, leaving his fortune exposed to the sharp fall in their value.CVR Energy, which accounts for roughly half of Icahn Enterprises' value, also came under pressure. Its shares fell 40% after a deal to acquire two refineries this month. Icahn's private funds, meanwhile, were down 43.8% through September after heavy losses on short positions against energy stocks and the broader market.$1.4 billion in bonds add to the pressureThe company's immediate challenge is its debt. Icahn Enterprises warned earlier this month that it might not be able to refinance $1.4 billion in bonds due in May on acceptable terms.The market reaction has been severe. Yields on those bonds have risen from 6% to more than 14% in three months, while yields on some of the company's 2029 bonds have climbed above 30%.Bond yields generally rise when investors become less willing to hold a company's debt, often demanding a higher return to compensate for the perceived risk. In Icahn Enterprises' case, the sharp increase reflects growing concern about the company's ability to meet its obligations and refinance its borrowings.The company has already sold assets to raise cash. It disposed of Pep Boys for about $700 million over the summer, but has warned that selling more assets quickly could result in steep losses.Hindenburg report intensified scrutinyIcahn's financial troubles gained fresh momentum in May 2023, when short-selling firm Hindenburg Research accused Icahn Enterprises of overstating the value of its assets and using what it described as "Ponzi-like" payouts to fund dividends.The allegations sent the company's shares down by more than half in a month. The report also drew attention to billions of dollars in personal margin loans secured against Icahn's company units and prompted a federal probe.Icahn rejected the report, calling it "scurrilous". In 2024, he and his company agreed to pay $2 million to settle Securities and Exchange Commission charges related to the disclosure of loans. They neither admitted nor denied wrongdoing as part of the settlement.Although Icahn later restructured the debt, the company's stock did not regain its earlier ground.A dealmaker facing resistanceThe financial strain has also complicated Icahn's ability to pursue major acquisitions. Earlier this year, Caesars Entertainment rejected his takeover bid, despite his offer reportedly being $3 per share higher than that of rival bidder Tilman Fertitta.Concerns over Icahn's personal loans and the financing behind his proposal reportedly weighed on the decision.The setbacks mark a sharp reversal for a financier who built his reputation on aggressive corporate takeovers, including battles involving RJR Nabisco and TWA. His influence once extended well beyond Wall Street: his name is attached to Icahn Stadium on Randall's Island and the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai.Icahn moved his firm's headquarters from Manhattan to Sunny Isles Beach, Florida, in 2020. He now lives in a waterfront mansion on Indian Creek Island.Icahn's old feud with Bill Ackman resurfacesIcahn's fortune has also fallen far behind that of his longtime rival Bill Ackman, whose net worth is estimated at $9.2 billion. The two investors have been locked in a bitter dispute for decades, with their feud tracing back to a 2003 real estate disagreement that ended with a $9 million court victory for Ackman.Their rivalry became a public spectacle in 2013 during a heated live CNBC exchange over nutrition company Herbalife. Icahn called Ackman "a crybaby" and "a major loser" during the confrontation.On Wednesday, Ackman, who is active on social media, limited his response to retweeting a news article about Icahn's falling fortune. A representative for Ackman did not respond to a request for comment, while attempts to reach Icahn by phone were unsuccessful.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.summary: Bihar CM Samrat Choudhary to hold two-day Patna meet with DMs, SPs to review scheme implementation, address bottlenecks, and assess law and order.
articles.body: Patna: CM Samrat Choudhary will hold a two-day high-level meeting with senior govt officials, district magistrates (DMs) and superintendents of police (SPs) from all districts in Patna from Saturday to review the implementation of govt schemes and discuss administrative and law and order issues.The meeting will feature presentations by various govt departments on their schemes and programmes. District-level officials will also be briefed on the initiatives being run by the govt to ensure their effective implementation and delivery of benefits to people.An official said the exercise would help DMs and other officers gain a better understanding of various schemes and their objectives, enabling them to ensure eligible beneficiaries receive the intended benefits.Sources said the CM would also take stock of law and order across the state. articles.title: DU moves to protect LLB students from losing original marks if they miss improvement exam
articles.summary: Delhi University lets LLB students keep original marks if they miss an applied-for improvement exam, following a case and VC Yogesh Singh’s June 1 order.
articles.body: New Delhi: LL.B students at Delhi University who missed an improvement examination after applying for it earlier risked losing their original marks as well, despite having cleared the paper in the first attempt. The university has now allowed their previous scores to be restored if students fail to appear for the improvement exam.The decision was taken by vice-chancellor Yogesh Singh on June 1, under his delegated powers. DU has now placed the decision before its academic council for information, along with an order to ratify the provision in the faculty of law’s information bulletin.In effect, this could leave a student with a backlog, potentially affecting academic progress and forcing them to wait until the next examination cycle to clear the paper, despite having passed it in the first attempt.The move follows a case involving a three-year LL.B student at the Campus Law Centre, who approached Delhi High Court after being marked absent in an improvement examination he could not appear for.The student, Prashant Attri, had scored 46 out of 100 in Constitutional Law-I (LB-301) in his semester III examinations in Jan 2025. During his semester V examinations, he filled up an improvement form for the paper but could not appear for the examination.However, when the semester V results were declared on Feb 24, he was marked absent in the improvement paper. His earlier marks were not restored. Attri challenged this, relying on Clause 8 of the Faculty of Law’s 2023-24 prospectus, which did not provide restoration of the original score if a student fails to clear the second attempt for any reason.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.body: Twitch streamer and CORE Boys member Nick “Lacy” faced criticism after a heated exchange with his moderator Rumz during a Thanksgiving livestream on November 26, 2026. Lacy questioned Rumz for taking time off and accused him of leaving work unfinished despite receiving a $2,000 bonus. The streamer also made harsh remarks about Rumz spending the holiday with his family. While some viewers believed the exchange was staged for clips, others criticized Lacy's comments. The same stream later took another turn when people were heard asking him to come outside with his hands up.Nick “Lacy” Questions Rumz's Thanksgiving Break and Makes Remarks About His FamilyLacy was streaming with his girlfriend, Darla, when he tried to contact Rumz. The moderator initially missed his call but called back a few minutes later. During their conversation, Rumz explained that he was in Barcelona and had taken paid time off under his contract.However, Lacy was unhappy with the arrangement. He brought up a $2,000 bonus he had given Rumz and questioned why his YouTube streams had not been set up for two days.At one point, Lacy said:"Yo, Rumz! ('Yo, what's up?') I'm live right now. Quick little question, buddy: You got your bonus and just quit or some ****? How's this work? ('I'm in Barcelona, dude. What do you want from me?.. I took my paid time off; it's in my contract.') Paid time off? I gave you a $2,000 bonus for four days, and you just quit on me. I haven't had a YouTube stream in two days! ('Listen, I'll get it all set up for you.')."The conversation became more heated when Lacy brought up Rumz's Thanksgiving plans. He said he did not care about the moderator's family commitments and expected him to work whenever he was told."Are you trying to spend Thanksgiving with your family today? ('Uhh') Well, too ******* bad! Too bad! I don't care about your family; you work when I say you work. You're on call when I say you're on call; that's what you get paid the big bucks for, buddy... I don't care about your family; **** your Thanksgiving! Get on the ToolKit! ('Yes, sir. I will fly back from vacation')."Lacy also addressed the criticism he received over the exchange. He claimed Rumz earned enough money to be available when needed and said the moderator was paid $7.25 an hour.The clip soon drew mixed reactions on X. Some viewers thought the argument was planned to create entertaining clips, while others felt Lacy had gone too far. One user, @ThisIsJaysol, wrote, "Clip farming like mf lol." Another user, @Fallking76, called it "Clip bait %100" and questioned whether anyone would behave that way on Thanksgiving.Others were less convinced that it was an act. @ADDICTED2GAM3S called Lacy a "Piece of 💩 human," while @bangacentral simply wrote, "Lacy wrong for that." However, there has been no confirmation that the exchange was staged.Nick “Lacy” Appears to Get Swatted While Streaming With DarlaThe argument with Rumz was not the only unexpected moment during Lacy's November 26 stream. Later, while spending Thanksgiving with Darla, the streamer appeared to face a swatting incident.Voices could be heard in the background telling him to come outside with his hands up. Lacy then followed the instructions and moved out of the camera's view.Afterward, he spoke about the person he believed was behind the incident. He criticized the viewer for allegedly involving real-life authorities while he was spending the holiday with his girlfriend."Imagine, chat, Thanksgiving, chilling with your family, swatting someone? Actual, like real-life, degenerate loser. Actual loser... (Sarcastically) 'Why would I hang out with my family when I could just swat a streamer?'"The incident appeared to interrupt what had been a Thanksgiving cooking stream with Darla. However, the available footage does not establish who made the call or confirm the identity of the person responsible.Meanwhile, Lacy and the other CORE Boys members had also organized a GTA 6 marathon earlier in November, bringing their gaming content to viewers through a series of livestreams.You use AI every day.
